rows.reference: Guru Granth Sahib, ang 1128, Rāg Bhairao, Guru Amar Das (Mahalla 3), second shabad of his Bhairao hymns (marker ||6||2||), stanza 3 (line 1128.6)
rows.original: ਸੋ ਜਾਗੈ ਜੋ ਤਤੁ ਬੀਚਾਰੈ ॥ ਆਪਿ ਮਰੈ ਅਵਰਾ ਨਹ ਮਾਰੈ ॥੩॥
rows.says: The person who is truly awake thinks about what is real. He dies to his own self (his self-conceit) and does not kill anyone else.
rows.bearing: K1 and K0: the most direct counted text found. It describes the awakened person, so it is a portrait, not a rule (Clear teaching). Its object, 'others' (avrā), has no limit of faith, sex, age or status. So it reaches everyone K1 protects, newborns included (rules 7 and 9). It has no exception for defence, so it asks more than K1, and as a wider rule it still counts (rule 7). Mārai can also mean 'strike'. On that reading the duty is wider still, and it still includes killing. A person who kills no one also kills no one for gain, anger or revenge, so it carries K0 as well.

rows.reference: Guru Granth Sahib, ang 356, Rāg Āsā, Guru Nanak (Mahalla 1), shabad marked ||4||25||, stanza 3 (lines 356.16 to 356.17)
rows.original: ਦਇਆ ਦਿਗੰਬਰੁ ਦੇਹ ਬੀਚਾਰੀ ॥ ਆਪਿ ਮਰੈ ਅਵਰਾ ਨਹ ਮਾਰੀ ॥੩॥
rows.says: The shabad redefines religious types by their inner conduct. The true naked ascetic (digambar) is the one who, through compassion, looks within. He slays his own self and does not slay others.
rows.bearing: K1 and K0: Guru Nanak states the same principle as ang 1128, in the same words. It says what true religion requires (compassion; not killing others). It is not a legal rule, so it is Clear teaching. Its setting is a set of ascetic ideals (sannyasi, yogi, digambar; the last is a Jain term), which could be read as an ideal for ascetics only. Ang 1128 says the same of anyone who is 'awake', so taken together they are not confined to ascetics. The object is unrestricted and there is no exception (wider rule, rule 7).

rows.reference: Guru Granth Sahib, ang 4, Japji, pauṛī 18 ('Asaṅkh mūrakh'), Guru Nanak (lines 4.3 to 4.5)
rows.original: ਅਸੰਖ ਗਲਵਢ ਹਤਿਆ ਕਮਾਹਿ ॥ ਅਸੰਖ ਪਾਪੀ ਪਾਪੁ ਕਰਿ ਜਾਹਿ ॥ ... ਨਾਨਕੁ ਨੀਚੁ ਕਹੈ ਵੀਚਾਰੁ
rows.says: The countless wrongdoers in creation include fools, thieves, those who force their will on others, cut-throats who commit murder (hatiā), sinners, liars and slanderers. Nanak says he is describing the state of the low (nīch).
rows.bearing: K1, supporting: the Japji is the opening and most recited composition of the Guru Granth Sahib, and it ranks murder with sin and wrongdoing. It names no class of victim and no exception, so it condemns killing anyone. It condemns by describing; it does not give a rule, so it supports and does not decide. It is not about courts or war.

rows.reference: Guru Granth Sahib, ang 1384, Saloks of Sheikh Farid 129 and 130 (lines 1384.17 to 1384.19)
rows.original: ਇਕੁ ਫਿਕਾ ਨ ਗਾਲਾਇ ਸਭਨਾ ਮੈ ਸਚਾ ਧਣੀ ॥ ਹਿਆਉ ਨ ਕੈਹੀ ਠਾਹਿ ਮਾਣਕ ਸਭ ਅਮੋਲਵੇ ॥੧੨੯॥ ਸਭਨਾ ਮਨ ਮਾਣਿਕ ਠਾਹਣੁ ਮੂਲਿ ਮਚਾਂਗਵਾ
rows.says: Do not speak even one harsh word, because the True Master lives in everyone. Do not break anyone's heart; all are priceless jewels. Salok 130: the minds of all are precious jewels, and to harm them is not good at all. If you long for the Beloved, break no one's heart.
rows.bearing: K1 and K0: a wider duty not to harm anyone, grounded in God's presence in every person. So it reaches newborns, women, servants, people of other faiths and wrongdoers alike (rules 7 and 9). Salok 130 states the duty not to harm (ṭhāhaṇ) in so many words. The project already counts it as a wider duty not to harm (Article I row 11a; households annex, L1 'do not injure'). It speaks of words and hearts, and it reaches killing as the gravest harm. Now that ang 1128 and 356 are verified, K1 no longer depends on this reading.

rows.reference: Guru Granth Sahib, ang 1102 to 1103, Rāg Mārū, Bhagat Kabir, first of Kabir's Mārū shabads (it opens at line 1102.19), stanza 2 (line 1103.2)
rows.original: ਜੀਅ ਬਧਹੁ ਸੁ ਧਰਮੁ ਕਰਿ ਥਾਪਹੁ ਅਧਰਮੁ ਕਹਹੁ ਕਤ ਭਾਈ ॥ ਆਪਸ ਕਉ ਮੁਨਿਵਰ ਕਰਿ ਥਾਪਹੁ ਕਾ ਕਉ ਕਹਹੁ ਕਸਾਈ ॥੨॥
rows.says: The shabad is addressed to a pandit who reads the Vedas and Puranas. You kill living beings and call it a righteous act; then, brother, what would you call unrighteous? You call yourself the best of sages; then whom would you call a butcher?
rows.bearing: K1 and K0: a polemic whose premise is that a religious label cannot make the killing of living beings (jīa, which includes people) righteous. As a wider rule it reaches people killed in the name of religion (unbelievers, heretics, 'the wicked'). Its setting is a Brahmin's sacrificial killing, and the tradition does not read Kabir's verses as a ban on all killing of animals (ang 1289 to 1290). So, as a rule about people, it is borderline. Supporting.

rows.reference: Guru Granth Sahib, ang 1375, Saloks of Bhagat Kabir, salok 199 (line 1375.5)
rows.original: ਕਬੀਰ ਜੀਅ ਜੁ ਮਾਰਹਿ ਜੋਰੁ ਕਰਿ ਕਹਤੇ ਹਹਿ ਜੁ ਹਲਾਲੁ ॥ ਦਫਤਰੁ ਦਈ ਜਬ ਕਾਢਿ ਹੈ ਹੋਇਗਾ ਕਉਨੁ ਹਵਾਲੁ ॥੧੯੯॥
rows.says: Some use force to kill living beings and call it lawful (halāl). When God calls for their account, what will become of them? It comes right after two saloks on the pilgrimage to Mecca (197 and 198).
rows.bearing: K1 and K0: a wider rule (rule 7) that killing living beings by force cannot be made lawful by a religious name. Its setting is ritual slaughter, so, as with ang 1103, it reaches people only on a borderline reading. Supporting; it changes no label.

rows.original: ਹੁਣਿ ਹੁਕਮੁ ਹੋਆ ਮਿਹਰਵਾਣ ਦਾ ॥ ਪੈ ਕੋਇ ਨ ਕਿਸੈ ਰਞਾਣਦਾ ॥ ਸਭ ਸੁਖਾਲੀ ਵੁਠੀਆ ਇਹੁ ਹੋਆ ਹਲੇਮੀ ਰਾਜੁ ਜੀਉ ॥੧੩॥
rows.says: Now the Merciful Lord has given his order: let no one chase after and attack anyone else. Let all live in peace under this gentle rule.
rows.bearing: K1 and K0: a universal statement that no one should attack anyone (rule 7). Its setting is allegorical. Earlier stanzas say the devotee has become master of the 'body-village' and taken the five rival passions prisoner (stanzas 4 to 6). So the 'gentle rule' can be read as an inner state, though Sikhs widely cite it as a picture of a just society. Hence borderline. Supporting; K1 does not depend on it.

rows.original: ਫਰੀਦਾ ਬੁਰੇ ਦਾ ਭਲਾ ਕਰਿ ਗੁਸਾ ਮਨਿ ਨ ਹਢਾਇ ॥ ਦੇਹੀ ਰੋਗੁ ਨ ਲਗਈ ਪਲੈ ਸਭੁ ਕਿਛੁ ਪਾਇ ॥੭੮॥

rows.original: ਫਰੀਦਾ ਜੋ ਤੈ ਮਾਰਨਿ ਮੁਕੀਆਂ ਤਿਨੑਾ ਨ ਮਾਰੇ ਘੁੰਮਿ ॥ ਆਪਨੜੈ ਘਰਿ ਜਾਈਐ ਪੈਰ ਤਿਨੑਾ ਦੇ ਚੁੰਮਿ ॥੭॥
rows.says: Do not turn round and strike those who hit you with their fists; kiss their feet and go home.

The tradition elsewhere accepts force as a last resort (Zafarnama row), so Sikh readers take it as counsel against retaliation, not as a ban on defending the weak. It does not contradict K1 or K0.

rows.original: ਬ੍ਰਹਮਣ ਕੈਲੀ ਘਾਤੁ ਕੰਞਕਾ ਅਣਚਾਰੀ ਕਾ ਧਾਨੁ ॥ ਫਿਟਕ ਫਿਟਕਾ ਕੋੜੁ ਬਦੀਆ ਸਦਾ ਸਦਾ ਅਭਿਮਾਨੁ ॥ ਪਾਹਿ ਏਤੇ ਜਾਹਿ ਵੀਸਰਿ ਨਾਨਕਾ ਇਕੁ ਨਾਮੁ
rows.translation: Sant Singh Khalsa (Shabad OS database), who glosses the list as 'the four Hindu cardinal sins' and renders kañjakā 'a female infant'
rows.says: The killing of a Brahmin, of a cow or of a girl (kañjakā), and eating the food of a wicked person; the world's curse, leprosy and endless pride: all these fall on the one who forgets the One Name.
rows.bearing: K1's 'from birth onwards' clause (rule 9), narrowly. It is the one counted text found that names the killing of a girl (in context, female infanticide) as among the gravest sins. The Guru takes over a traditional list (Brahmin, cow, girl) to show how grave it is to forget the Name, so the condemnation is assumed rather than argued; hence borderline. Kañjakā means a girl or maiden; 'infant' is the translator's reading. It does not say that killing other people is a lesser wrong, so it states no graded protection. It corrects the earlier finding that no Guru Granth Sahib verse names infanticide. Alongside ang 1128 and 356, it supports reading K1's protection as reaching newborn girls.
rows.strength: Clear teaching (narrow: killing a girl is a grave sin), borderline

rows.original: ਏਤੀ ਮਾਰ ਪਈ ਕਰਲਾਣੇ ਤੈਂ ਕੀ ਦਰਦੁ ਨ ਆਇਆ ॥ ਜੇ ਸਕਤਾ ਸਕਤੇ ਕਉ ਮਾਰੇ ਤਾ ਮਨਿ ਰੋਸੁ ਨ ਹੋਈ ॥ ਸਕਤਾ ਸੀਹੁ ਮਾਰੇ ਪੈ ਵਗੈ ਖਸਮੈ ਸਾ ਪੁਰਸਾਈ (ang 360); ਪਾਪ ਕੀ ਜੰਞ ਲੈ ਕਾਬਲਹੁ ਧਾਇਆ ... ਖੂਨ ਕੇ ਸੋਹਿਲੇ ਗਾਵੀਅਹਿ ਨਾਨਕ (ang 722 to 723)
rows.says: Guru Nanak laments Babur's invasion. The people screamed under the slaughter: did You feel no pity? If the strong strike the strong, no one grieves; but if a tiger falls on a flock and kills, its master must answer. Dogs have laid waste a priceless land, and no one cares for the dead (ang 360). Babur came from Kabul with 'a marriage party of sin', taking by force. Muslim and Hindu women of every rank suffered alike; 'wedding songs of murder' are sung, and blood is sprinkled instead of saffron (ang 722 to 723). Women were shorn, dishonoured and carried off, and princes were cut down, while the battle between the Mughal and Pathan armies is reported without complaint (ang 417 to 418). The hymns also say God sent the Mughal as the messenger of death and that whatever pleases God comes to pass.
rows.bearing: K3: the hymns draw K3's line. Fighting between armed equals is not complained of. The slaughter of the defenceless 'flock', and of women of every faith and rank, is called sin and murder. This is Clear teaching through lament, but borderline: it is addressed to God, it is not a rule for fighters, and it frames the invasion as divine judgement. That framing is not approval of the killers (the same hymns call the act sin), so rule 4 does not turn it into a contradiction. It does not mention those who surrender. War is context only for K1 and K0 (rule 5).

rows.reference: Guru Granth Sahib, whole text (Shabad OS database, 1,430 angs): searches of the English for kill, slay, slaughter, murder, butcher, behead and annihilate, and of the Gurmukhi for ਮਾਰ, ਹਤਿਆ, ਘਾਤ, ਬਧ, ਖੂਨ, ਦੁਸਟ, ਨਿੰਦਕ, ਖੜਗ, ਤੇਗ and ਜੁਧ
rows.says: About 200 lines speak of killing. They fall into these groups: God kills and revives (for example ang 125, 150, 1069); killing the ego, the mind, the five passions or Death (for example ang 237 to 238, 1364, 1414); God destroys slanderers and the wicked (row above); Hindu stories of God slaying demons (ang 224, 1105, 1194); polemics against killing living beings (ang 332, 483, 662, 1103, 1350, 1375); condemnations of murderers, with God's mercy to them if they repent (ang 4, 70, 316, 493, 651); laments of war (ang 360, 417 to 418, 722 to 723); one statement that sword-fighting happens by God's will (ang 145); and two verses on not killing others (ang 356, 1128).
rows.bearing: No line was found in which a person, acting on their own authority, is permitted, commanded or praised for killing a person, or in which a killing is declared blameless because of who the victim is. This is a keyword search of one dataset, not a reading of every line, so a passage phrased without these words could have been missed.

corrections: Direct reading: every Guru Granth Sahib passage cited in the rows was read in the Shabad OS database (gurbani.py, with Sant Singh Khalsa's English). All Tier 1 rows are now VERIFIED (direct). The Sikh Rehat Maryada, the Dasam Granth, the Vaaran Bhai Gurdas and the outside-corpus items are not local, so their statuses were kept.

Two new deciding texts found by a full-text search: ang 1128 (Guru Amar Das, Rāg Bhairao) and ang 356 (Guru Nanak, Rāg Āsā). Both say the true person 'dies to himself and does not kill others' (āp marai avrā nah mārai). They speak of not killing others in so many words, so K1 no longer rests on ang 1384 and 1103 alone and is no longer borderline.

K1.label: Not contradicted; taught (Clear teaching, wider rule)
K1.reason: Deciding texts (Guru Granth Sahib, Tier 1, accepted by every Sikh group, all read directly): ang 1128 (Guru Amar Das: the one who is awake 'dies to himself and does not kill others') and ang 356 (Guru Nanak: the true ascetic, through compassion, 'slays his own self, not others'). They are portraits of the right way to live, not legal rules, so they are Clear teaching. Their object, 'others', is unrestricted, so they reach every person K1 protects, newborns included (rules 7 and 9). They have no defence exception, so they are wider than K1 and count under rule 7. Supporting texts, all read directly: Japji 18 (ang 4: murderers listed among the wicked); Farid 129 to 130 (ang 1384: harm no one, because God is in all); Kabir at ang 1103, 1375 and 332 (killing living beings cannot be made righteous or lawful; borderline because of their sacrificial and slaughter settings, which ang 1289 to 1290 narrows as regards animals); ang 74 (let no one attack anyone; borderline, allegorical); ang 1427 (frighten no one); and, for newborn girls, ang 1413 (killing a girl is among the gravest sins; borderline). Counter-evidence: a full-text sweep found no counted line that permits, commands or praises a killing by a person acting on their own authority, or that declares a killing blameless because of who the victim is. The only approved killings are God's: Sulhi (ang 825), Harnakhas (ang 451, 1133, 1165, 1194 and others) and slanderers and the wicked (ang 199, 133, 533 and others). Rule 4 covers them, and most are framed as rescue from an attacker. Ang 145 ('we wield the sword ... when it pleases You') reports events under God's will and ends by calling them falsehood (rule 4). Kabir's ang 1105 is set on the battlefield (rule 5). The sākat saloks (ang 1371, 1372) say to keep away and never to harm. No Sikh authority narrows ang 1128 or 356, so rule 6 does not apply. Residual caution: both deciding texts are portraits, and mārai can also mean 'strike'; but both readings include killing, so the label stands. Cross-tradition hard cases: the Sikh counted texts have no counterpart to a kinsman allowed to kill a manslayer (Numbers 35:26 to 27), a zealot rewarded for killing (Phinehas), a master excused for killing a slave (Abū Dāwūd 4361), drowning weak newborns (De Ira 1.15.2), killing a class of people without retribution (the icchantika), or wronging the follower of the Lie (Yasna 31.18, 33.2). The nearest analogues are outside the corpus (Massa Ranghar's killing, Rahitnamas) or are Tier 2 prayers that God destroy enemies (Benti Chaupai), and none is counted. The Sikh Rehat Maryada's explicit ban on killing daughters is Tier 2 and is reported beside the label. Branches: every row that decides is accepted by all branches. If the Nihang orders or the Damdami Taksal were treated as a branch holding the Dasam Granth as primary (not decided under decisions 3 and 4), its war texts are prayers or battle narratives (rules 4 and 5), and K1 would not change.

K0.label: Not contradicted; taught (Clear teaching, wider rule)
K0.reason: Whatever teaches K1 also teaches K0, the narrower wording: a person who kills no one kills no one for gain, anger, hatred or revenge (ang 1128 and 356, with ang 1384). In addition, counted texts read directly address K0's motives as duties owed to everyone, wrongdoers included. Farid 78 (ang 1381 to 1382): answer evil with good and do not let anger fill your mind (anger and revenge). Farid 7 (ang 1378): do not strike back at those who hit you (revenge). Sahaskritī 27 (ang 1356): saints treat alike whoever feeds them and whoever comes at them with weapons (hatred and revenge). Ang 386: keep no ill will towards anyone (hatred). Sahaskritī 47 (ang 1358): anger is the root of strife (supporting). On gain, ang 199 (God burns the oppressor of the poor) and ang 141 (another's due is forbidden) are Implied only, but the gain limb is carried by the K1 texts as a wider rule. No counted text approves killing for gain, anger, hatred or revenge. This label is firmer than K1's because the motive texts are direct.

K3.label: Not contradicted; taught (Clear teaching), borderline
K3.reason: Deciding text: Guru Nanak's Babarvani (Tier 1, all branches, read directly). Ang 360 draws K3's line. If the strong strike the strong, no one grieves; but if a tiger falls on a flock and kills, the master must answer. The invaders are 'dogs' who laid waste the land. Ang 722 to 723 calls Babur's invasion 'a marriage party of sin' and speaks of 'songs of murder', with Muslim and Hindu women of every rank suffering alike. Ang 417 to 418 laments women dishonoured and carried off and princes cut down, while the battle between the two armies is reported without complaint. So the slaughter of the defenceless in war is condemned as sin and murder, and fighting between armed men is not: Clear teaching through lament. It is borderline for three reasons. It is a lament addressed to God, not a rule for fighters. It frames the invasion as divine judgement ('sent the Mughal as the messenger of death'; 'whatever pleases Him comes to pass'). And it does not mention those who surrender. The framing as divine judgement is not approval of the killers, because the same hymns call the act sin, so rule 4 does not turn it into a contradiction. A reviewer who held that a lament cannot be Clear teaching would make K3 'silent', not 'contradicted'. No counted text approves killing people who are not fighting. Ang 145 (heads cut off by the sword 'when it pleases' God) reports events and ends by calling them falsehood. Ang 1105 praises steadfastness in battle and says nothing about non-combatants. Tier 2, reported only: the Zafarnama's last-resort rule and its complaint of broken oaths of safe conduct (Implied support). The Dasam Granth's battle narratives and the Benti Chaupai's mleccha line are unverified (two searches in this pass failed) and not counted.

objections.label: K3
objections.objection: Ang 360 is misread as 'drawing K3's line'. In Gurmukhi the 'master' who must answer (ਖਸਮੈ ਸਾ ਪੁਰਸਾਈ, 360.14) is God, addressed in the line before: 'ਕਰਤਾ ਤੂੰ ਸਭਨਾ ਕਾ ਸੋਈ' (360.13, 'O Creator Lord, You are the Master of all'), and the stanza opens 'Didn't You feel compassion, Lord?' (360.13). The tiger is a predator, not a moral agent. So the strong-against-strong versus tiger-on-the-flock contrast is a complaint to God about His duty to protect the flock (a theodicy), not a teaching about what fighters may do. The proposed reason paraphrases 'the master must answer' without saying who the master is, and so turns a reproach addressed to God into a rule of war. Ang 722 to 723 (read directly) condemns Babur's invasion as a whole: 'marriage party of sin', demanding gifts 'by force' (ਜੋਰੀ), 'Satan conducts the rites', 'songs of murder', 'city of corpses'. That condemns one aggressor's war and its bloodshed. It does not single out the killing of people who are not fighting from the killing of fighters, and it does not bind a defending army. Taken alone, the Babarvani is a lament addressed to God with no rule for fighters: Implied for K3, or at most 'taught in part' (it reaches aggressors only).
objections.rule_basis: Rule 7 (taught means the wording is taught at Explicit or Clear teaching level; a duty that reaches only some of those the wording covers is 'taught in part'); METHOD.md section 3 (Clear teaching must not be stretched); rule 4 (a lament that reports and grieves does not state a rule).
objections.proposed: Rate the Babarvani for K3 as Implied (supporting), noting that ang 722 to 723 would at most teach K3 in part (aggressors). On the proposal's own basis K3 would then be 'Not contradicted; silent'. The label can be kept as 'taught, borderline' only by resting it on the wider rules (next objection).

objections.label: K3
objections.objection: The reason ignores the route that the K1 reasoning itself uses. K1 counts ang 1128 and 356 because their object, 'others' (ਅਵਰਾ), has no limit and they have no exception. The same logic reaches people who are not fighting in war: whoever kills no one kills no non-combatant (METHOD.md section 3, wider rules). Treating these lines as reaching every newborn for K1 but not testing them for K3 is inconsistent. The tradition's acceptance of fighting narrows them at most as to fighters, which K3 leaves open. This rests on ang 1105 on a literal reading of dīn, which the project's own translation reads as a spiritual battle ('the battle-drum beats in the sky of the mind', 1105.4), and on the Zafarnama, which is Tier 2 and verified only on secondary sites. No counted or Tier 2 text carves out non-combatants. The Zafarnama's complaint about broken oaths of safe conduct points the other way. So K3 is taught as a wider rule. It is borderline because both texts are portraits of personal conduct, not set in war, and their reach into war is inferred. Ang 1128's portrait is not confined to ascetics: the shabad names householders and 'whoever of the four castes' remains awake (1128.4, 1128.7).
objections.rule_basis: Rule 7 and METHOD.md section 3 (a wider rule counts if it reaches everyone the wording protects); rule 6 (only counted texts, classical commentators or an authorised body narrow; the Zafarnama is none of these, and ang 1105's narrowing depends on a disputed word); consistency with the K1 reasoning.
objections.proposed: Base K3 on ang 1128 and 356 as wider rules, with the Babarvani as Implied support. Label: 'Not contradicted; taught (Clear teaching, wider rule), borderline'. Record that a reviewer who holds that portraits of personal conduct do not reach war would make K3 'silent', never 'contradicted'.

objections.label: K3
objections.objection: Ang 417 to 418 is misread as setting lamented women against a battle 'reported without complaint'. Read directly, aṣṭpadī 12 reports the battle (418.2), then the dead 'whose letters were torn in the Lord's Court' and who 'were destined to die' (418.3), then the women (418.3 to 418.4), all in the same register. It ends: 'Pleasure and pain come by Your Will ... The Commander issues His Command, and is pleased' (418.5 to 418.6). Aṣṭpadī 11 has 'the order was given to the soldiers, who dishonored them, and carried them away. If it pleases Him ... He bestows punishment' (417.7 to 417.8, ਦੂਤਾ ਨੋ ਫੁਰਮਾਇਆ, with no stated agent). The only sin it names belongs to the defeated rulers: their wealth 'was not gathered without sin', and 'those whom the Creator would destroy, He first strips of virtue' (417.17 to 417.18). These hymns therefore frame the suffering of the defenceless as divine punishment, and they are the hardest counter-evidence for K3, not support for it. Rule 4 still keeps them from contradicting K3: no human killer is approved, the agent of 'furmāiā' is not stated, and ang 722 to 723 calls the same invasion sin.
objections.rule_basis: Rule 4 (reporting is not approving, unless God within the text says the act was right); MANDATORY counter-evidence and no cherry-picking (CLAUDE.md section 5).
objections.proposed: Move ang 417 to 418 to counter-evidence for K3, quoting 417.7 to 417.8, 417.17 to 417.18 and 418.3 to 418.6. Resolve it under rule 4 by pointing to ang 722 to 723 ('sin', 'Satan', 'murder') and 360.15 (the invaders are 'dogs'). Drop the claim that the battle is reported 'without complaint' as a contrast.

The slanderer verses are not framed as defence, so it is God's agency, not the exception, that keeps them from deciding. No counted line permits a person to carry out such a killing.' challenge.consistency_notes: Against the cross-tradition hard cases, the Sikh counted texts were checked for each kind of passage. Numbers 35:26 to 27 (a kinsman lawfully kills a manslayer): no Sikh counted text lets a kinsman or any private person kill. Phinehas: the nearest Sikh case (the killing of Massa Ranghar) is outside the corpus and decides nothing. Abū Dāwūd 4361 (a master excused for killing): no counted text excuses a master, parent or husband. In the Prahlad story the parent who tries to kill his child is the tyrant, and God rescues the child. De Ira 1.15.2 (drowning weak newborns): no counterpart. The Guru Granth Sahib names the killing of a girl only inside a borrowed Hindu list (ang 1413, Implied), and the explicit ban is Tier 2 (Rehat Maryada), reported beside the label. The icchantika passage (a human killing of a class declared free of retribution): the Sikh verses on the death of slanderers, the sākat and 'the wicked' are always acts of God, often after the fact, and never a licence to a person. This is the line that matters, so these verses should be set aside on K1's scope (it binds persons; rule 2), not on rule 4, whose exception they meet. The same ground should be used for God's killings in every tradition. Yasna 31.18 and 33.2 (resisting or wronging the follower of the Lie): the Sikh counterpart, Kabir's sākat saloks, counsels only avoidance, and Farid counsels not striking back. Atharvaveda rites against enemies and Bṛhadāraṇyaka 6.4.12: no Sikh counted text has a person perform a rite or petition God to kill. The Guru Granth Sahib lines (ang 201, 517, 523, 869, 1270) are thanksgiving or descriptions of God acting. The only petition, the Benti Chaupai, is Tier 2 and unverified. If it were ever counted, the line drawn between 'asking God to act' and 'a rite by which a person sets out to kill' must be drawn the same way for Hinduism. Rating portraits of the ideal person (ang 1128, 356, 1427, Sahaskritī 27) as Clear teaching matches how sayings and character portraits are rated for Taoism, Confucianism and Stoicism. For K3, a lament addressed to God that states no rule for fighters (the Babarvani) should be rated as laments are elsewhere, Implied. A universal duty not to kill with no war exception should count as a wider rule for K3 here exactly as it does in any tradition where such a duty is used for K3. Applying it to K1 but not to K3 would be inconsistent.
